content: Oxacillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. It is available as a liquid that is injected into a muscle or a blood vessel. The most common side effects of oxacillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site, as well as rashes. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect any adverse reactions. You can also report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 1-866-234-2345. Serious side effects of oxacillin, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, blood disorders, and liver damage. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, hives, dizziness, or fainting, stop using oxacillin and seek immediate medical attention. Seizures may present as muscle twitching, jerking, tremors, or loss of consciousness. Kidney damage symptoms include reduced urination, swelling in the legs or feet, and unusual fatigue. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile bacteria, can result in watery or persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Blood disorders may manifest as fever, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising, or frequent infections. Liver damage symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes), dark urine, or light-colored stools. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Oxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19. Misusing antibiotics, such as using them for non-bacterial infections, can lead to antibiotic resistance, making future bacterial infections harder to treat. Before using oxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about any allergies, especially to penicillin or other medications, as well as any history of asthma, liver or kidney problems, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Additionally, disclose all medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as oxacillin may interact with certain drugs, such as tetracyclines or probenecid. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss this with your healthcare provider. It is not known if oxacillin affects pregnancy or harms an unborn baby, but it does pass into breast milk. There are no known interactions between oxacillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption may weaken your immune response and hinder your body’s ability to fight infections. If you miss a dose of oxacillin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double doses. Complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to prevent antibiotic resistance. In case of an overdose, seek immediate medical help by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222.
